correct_citation: Roorda, D. L., Koomen, H. M. Y., Spilt, J. L., & Oort, F. J. (2011). The influence of affective teacher-student relationships on students' school engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic approach. Review of Educational Research, 81(4), 493-529. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654311421793
design: Meta-analysis of 99 studies (correlational associations). The abstract says some associations stayed significant 'after correction for methodological biases' but does not say whether longitudinal studies or controls for prior achievement were analysed separately. Full text not reachable (closed access).
population_location: Students preschool to high school; k=61 (N=52,718) positive TSR-achievement; k=28 (N=18,944) negative TSR-achievement; international
effect_as_reported: Associations with achievement small to medium; with engagement medium to large; stronger in higher grades
excerpt: Overall, associations of both positive and negative relationships with engagement were medium to large, whereas associations with achievement were small to medium. Some of these associations were weaker, but still statistically significant, after correction for methodological biases.
note: Association with achievement is confirmed. The design detail the claim asks about (longitudinal subset, prior-achievement controls) is not stated in the fetched abstract; treat as cross-sectional/correlational pooled evidence unless the full text is checked. The 2017 update (R-02) is the one that reports a longitudinal subsample.

correct_citation: Roorda, D. L., Jak, S., Zee, M., Oort, F. J., & Koomen, H. M. Y. (2017). Affective teacher-student relationships and students' engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic update and test of the mediating role of engagement. School Psychology Review, 46(3), 239-261.
design: Meta-analysis (meta-analytic structural equation modeling) of 189 studies, with a separate longitudinal subsample. The abstract does not say whether the longitudinal analyses control for prior achievement.
population_location: 249,198 students, preschool to high school; primary and secondary school
effect_as_reported: Associations of positive and negative TSRs with achievement partially mediated by engagement; partial mediation also in the longitudinal subsample (no coefficients in abstract)
excerpt: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling showed that, overall, the associations between both positive relationships and achievement and negative relationships and achievement were partially mediated by student engagement. ... Finally, partial mediation was also found in the longitudinal subsample.
note: Longitudinal associations are reported, as claimed. Do not describe them as adjusted for prior achievement; the abstract does not say so.

correct_citation: Jeynes, W. H. (2007). The relationship between parental involvement and urban secondary school student academic achievement: A meta-analysis. Urban Education, 42(1), 82-110. https://doi.org/10.1177/0042085906293818
design: Meta-analysis of 52 studies. Whether it reports results for studies with sophisticated controls is not stated in the abstract; full text closed (publisher 403, no ERIC full text).
population_location: Urban secondary school students, US; 52 studies
outcome: Overall academic achievement, grades, standardized tests, other measures (teacher ratings, academic attitudes and behaviors)
effect_as_reported: About 0.5 to 0.55 SD across academic variables; positive effects for White and minority students
excerpt: Parental involvement as a whole affects all the academic variables under study by about .5 to .55 of a standard deviation unit. The positive effects of parental involvement hold for both White and minority children.
note: Citation and main association confirmed from the abstract (Crossref and ERIC). The sophisticated-controls analysis could not be checked from fetched text, so no claim about adjusted estimates should rest on this verification. Abstract uses causal wording ('affects') for pooled mostly correlational studies.

correct_citation: Mahoney, J. L., & Cairns, R. B. (1997). Do extracurricular activities protect against early school dropout? Developmental Psychology, 33(2), 241-253. https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.33.2.241
fetched_url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=9147833&rettype=abstract&retmode=text (PubMed 9147833; the PubMed web page itself returned a cookie wall)
design: Longitudinal (annual follow-up grade 7 to 12). Students grouped by middle-school social-academic competence clusters (teacher ratings); the abstract does not report statistical adjustment for prior achievement or attendance.
population_location: 392 adolescents (206 girls, 186 boys), followed from 7th grade; US (University of North Carolina study)
outcome: Early school dropout (failure to complete 11th grade)
effect_as_reported: Dropout markedly lower among at-risk students who earlier participated (p < .001); only modest relation among competent students
excerpt: Findings indicate that the school dropout rate among at-risk students was markedly lower for students who had earlier participated in extracurricular activities compared with those who did not participate (p < .001).
note: Matches the claim, including the stronger link for higher-risk students. Risk is a stratifying cluster, not a covariate-adjusted baseline.

correct_citation: Thouin, E., Dupere, V., Dion, E., McCabe, J., Denault, A.-S., Archambault, I., Briere, F. N., et al. (2020/2022). School-based extracurricular activity involvement and high school dropout among at-risk students: Consistency matters. Applied Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2020.1796665
design: Matched case-control within a screened cohort: students screened early in the year for dropout risk (N=6,773); recent dropouts interviewed and each matched to a persevering peer from the same school, sector and sex with the closest risk score; ECA involvement in the past 12 months reported at interview (retrospective). Regressions control for confounders including initial dropout risk. Authors call the design correlational. Not a multi-year longitudinal cohort.
population_location: High-risk sample, N=545, 12 low-income high schools in Quebec, Canada
effect_as_reported: Consistent involvement in past year: OR = 0.32 (95% CI 0.17-0.61) for dropout; interrupted involvement carried similar risk to no involvement
excerpt: following a matched case-control logic ... a second interview was conducted with a persevering student from the same school, sector (regular or special education) and sex who showed the closest dropout risk score
note: Finding confirmed (abstract: 'consistent involvement in the past year was associated with lower odds of dropout (OR = 0.32; 95% CI = 0.17-0.61)'). Prior risk is handled by matching and controls, as claimed, but 'longitudinal study' overstates the design: one-year matched case-control with retrospective activity reports.

correct_citation: Valentine, J. C., DuBois, D. L., & Cooper, H. (2004). The relation between self-beliefs and academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Educational Psychologist, 39(2), 111-133.
design: Meta-analysis of longitudinal studies; effect is the path/regression coefficient of self-beliefs on later achievement controlling for initial achievement.
population_location: Longitudinal studies of students (abstract gives no population detail)
effect_as_reported: Average standardized path/regression coefficient .08; stronger when self-beliefs are academic-domain-specific and matched by domain
excerpt: Estimated effects are consistent with a small, favorable influence of positive self-beliefs on academic achievement, with an average standardized path or regression coefficient of .08 for self-beliefs as a predictor of later achievement, controlling for initial levels of achievement.
note: Design and effect exactly as claimed.

correct_citation: Marsh, H. W., & Craven, R. G. (2006). Reciprocal effects of self-concept and performance from a multidimensional perspective: Beyond seductive pleasure and unidimensional perspectives. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 1(2), 133-163. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-6916.2006.00010.x
fetched_url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=26151468&rettype=abstract&retmode=text (claim URL https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:96252694-a5df-4af1-9db3-274c990293f6 is a different paper: Marsh & O'Mara 2008)
design: Narrative review of reciprocal-effects-model (REM) longitudinal studies plus a cited meta-analysis; REM models estimate effects of prior self-concept and prior achievement on later outcomes, so each path is adjusted for the prior level of the other.

effect_as_reported: No pooled coefficient in abstract; prior academic self-concept and achievement both have positive effects on subsequent self-concept and achievement
excerpt: research based on our reciprocal-effects model (REM) and a recent meta-analysis show that prior academic self-concept (as opposed to self-esteem) and achievement both have positive effects on subsequent self-concept and achievement.
note: Fix the URL: the given ORA record is Marsh & O'Mara (2008), Reciprocal effects ... over seven adolescent years (Youth in Transition, N=2,213), which cites Marsh & Craven (2006). Use DOI 10.1111/j.1745-6916.2006.00010.x / PubMed 26151468. Secondary review, not one primary study.

correct_citation: Jackson, C. K., Porter, S. C., Easton, J. Q., Blanchard, A., & Kiguel, S. (2020). School effects on socioemotional development, school-based arrests, and educational attainment. NBER Working Paper 26759; published in American Economic Review: Insights, 2(4), 491-508.
design: Quasi-experimental school value-added (leave-year-out) on administrative and survey data; conditions on lagged 7th and 8th grade test scores, surveys, discipline, attendance and demographics; selection tests reported.
outcome: Self-reported SED (social well-being index incl. School Connectedness and interpersonal skills; hard-work index), school-based arrests, high school completion, college-going, college persistence
effect_as_reported: SED value-added more predictive of longer-run impacts than test-score value-added; using both more than doubles explained variance of school effects on longer-run outcomes
excerpt: Conditional on schools' test score impacts, schools that improve SED reduce school-based arrests, and increase high-school completion, college-going, and college persistence. ... school SED value-added is more predictive of school impacts on longer-run outcomes than school test-score value-added.
note: Matches the claim. There are two indices (social well-being, which includes school connectedness, and hard work) rather than one socioemotional index.

correct_citation: Jackson, C. K. (2018). What do test scores miss? The importance of teacher effects on non-test score outcomes. Journal of Political Economy, 126(5), 2072-2107. (NBER Working Paper 22226, 2016)
design: Quasi-experimental teacher value-added; all models include lagged outcomes (math and reading scores, repeater status, suspensions and attendance in 7th and 8th grade, 8th-grade GPA) and demographics; author presents tests for causal interpretation.
population_location: All public school 9th graders in North Carolina, 2005-2012 (11,857 math and English teachers)
outcome: Behavior index (grades, on-time grade progression, absences, suspensions); high school graduation, dropout, SAT-taking, college plans
effect_as_reported: 1 SD in teacher behavior-index effect raises graduation likelihood by 1.47 percentage points (vs 0.12 for test-score value-added in the joint model); including both more than doubles predictable teacher-level variability
excerpt: Teacher effects on these non-test-score outcomes in 9th grade predict effects on high-school completion and predictors of college-going—above and beyond their effects on test scores.
note: Matches the claim; behavior index components exactly as stated.
